articles.title: Your favorite Thanksgiving dishes won’t cost substantially more this year – here’s why
articles.author: Elizabeth Canales, Associate Professor of Agricultural Economics, Mississippi State University
paras: Inflation-weary Americans have at least some good news to cheer this holiday season: The cost of a basic Thanksgiving meal has stabilized.

A Thanksgiving dinner for 10 people clocks in at US$78.93, approximately 0.4% less than in 2025, according to the Wells Fargo Agri-Food Institute. That’s because most staples haven’t seen a sharp jump in prices.

Americans are still justified in feeling stressed about high grocery bills, but it’s because of the cumulative effect of rising prices in recent years. While inflation has slowed since its peak of more than 9% in 2022, the cost of a Thanksgiving meal is roughly 25% higher than it was before the COVID-19 pandemic began.

I’m an agricultural economist who has been studying the many drivers of food inflation. What’s key to remember is that inflation data tells us how quickly prices are increasing, not whether prices are returning to previous levels. So even modest price jumps today are layered on already-elevated prices.
Here’s what Americans can expect when they go shopping for Thanksgiving, from turkey to dessert:
Stable frozen turkey prices have played an important role in keeping overall holiday meal costs close to last year’s levels.

The average advertised price for a frozen turkey over 16 pounds (about 7 kilograms) was $0.96 per pound, essentially unchanged from the $0.97 per pound in the same period last year, according to the USDA Agricultural Marketing Service’s Weekly Turkey Report, published on Nov. 13, 2026. These prices reflect the typical discounts leading up to Thanksgiving, when retailers often cut turkey prices as part of their holiday promotions.

It’s a different story with fresh turkey prices, which are about 11% higher than a year ago, according to the Department of Agriculture data. So shoppers seeking a fresh bird may face a higher grocery bill.

A longer-term trend is that turkey consumption has gradually declined over time. As a result, the cost of Thanksgiving depends on much more than turkey prices alone. This is where side dishes come in.
A mixed picture for side dishes
Mashed potatoes, cranberry sauce and sweet potato casserole are among the dishes that a frugal shopper might consider.
Sweet potatoes are 12.5% cheaper year on year, and cranberry prices have dropped 4.8%, according to the USDA Agricultural Marketing Service’s Weekly Grocery Store Specialty Crops data.

Potato prices, meanwhile, have been stable, increasing just 1.1% over the past year, according to September’s consumer price index, the most recent month of full data. If you’re considering mac and cheese, the costs of the main ingredients should balance out: Pasta and cornmeal prices are 4.3% higher year on year, while cheese is 3% cheaper.

Prices for fruits and vegetables, however, have mostly ticked upward and are 3.9% higher than a year ago. That includes green beans, which are 2.2% more expensive. Prices for fresh apples are up 7.5%, and up 2.6% for lettuce.

More broadly, higher prices for some fresh vegetables reflect the cost pressures facing food production. Farmers are grappling with high fertilizer, fuel and transportation expenses, not to mention tariffs in certain sectors.

Of course, Thanksgiving isn’t complete without regional traditions. Sauerkraut is a popular side dish for turkey in the mid-Atlantic states, but fans will have to pay substantially more. Cabbage is about 30% more expensive year on year due to weather shocks and pest outbreaks that have reduced supply.
Americans might also find some sweet relief in prices for popular desserts.

Some key baking staples became more affordable. Butter prices have fallen 10.3% over the previous year, while flour is down by 1.1% and sugar by 1%, according to the September consumer price index data.

But some of the biggest savings come from eggs, where prices have dropped sharply. Like the turkey industry, egg production was hard-hit in 2022 by a highly pathogenic avian flu outbreak, which reduced supplies and pushed prices up. Since then, producers have rebuilt flocks and expanded production to grow supply. Egg prices are now 20.3% lower than a year ago.

Where consumers will shell out more is milk, up 2.3%; canned fruit, up 2.3%; and frozen bakery products, up 1.3%, according to the consumer price index data. Pumpkins for pie-making will cost 2% more than last year.
So keep all this in mind if you plan to bake a pie. And if you opt for a store-bought pumpkin pie, expect to pay about 2.5% more.
Where other savings can be found

Shoppers looking for alternatives to turkey could head to the poultry aisle. Prices for whole fryer and roaster chickens are anywhere from 7% to 20% lower than a year ago, according to USDA grocery store price data.

Consumers can also take advantage of Thanksgiving promotions offered by grocery retailers. Several major retailers offer complete Thanksgiving meal baskets for less than $40, which can translate to approximately $3.50 to $4 per person. Among major retailers, Walmart is advertising its Thanksgiving basket for 10 people at $35, Aldi at $39 for 10 people and Target at $30 for six people.
Although the contents vary, these meal packages generally include Thanksgiving favorites such as turkey, stuffing and cranberry sauce, and ingredients for green bean and potato side dishes.

Inflation remains at the top of consumers’ minds, and it isn’t expected to ease anytime soon. But in the case of Thanksgiving, shoppers can find at least some relief as they seek out staples for their feast.
Elizabeth Canales receives funding from the U.S. Department of Agriculture and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

articles.title: The philosophical reason AI Christmas ads leave audiences feeling cold
articles.author: Alex Fisher, Postdoctoral Fellow, University of Leeds
paras: It’s that time of year when Christmas adverts start appearing, and brands offer up a slice of consumerist comfort as you curl up in front of a screen.

Yet companies are increasingly using artificial intelligence (AI) to produce their ads. Last year proved how quickly that strategy can backfire. In the Netherlands, McDonald’s pulled an AI-generated Christmas ad depicting chaotic holiday mishaps after just three days following fierce backlash over the undisclosed usage.

This kind of omission is now restricted under new EU transparency rules that govern how AI-generated content is labelled. Coca-Cola’s 2025 festive campaign drew similar criticism. The advert featured AI-generated scenery and animals that many viewers found uncanny.

Undeterred, this year brands including Very and Plusnet have pressed ahead with AI productions. Because UK law does not require on-screen disclosure, their use of the technology is often tucked away in separate press releases and trade announcements rather than flagged to viewers. Even so, the UK Advertising Standards Authority prohibits misleading omissions if an advert falsely implies human creation to deceive consumers.

Other brands are more subtle with their AI use. While Royal Mail’s 2025 Christmas ad relied on traditional live-action footage, it recently emerged that the campaign used an AI voiceover to narrate the spot.

Replacing human performers – even behind the microphone – has fuelled growing anxiety among both industry insiders and the general public, echoing the fears that sparked the 2023 Hollywood writers’ and actors’ strikes.
Losing trust in animated ads

This growing scepticism means even traditional animation is no longer safe from scrutiny. Dior’s Christmas short film, for example, has generated suspicions among some viewers. Described as hand-drawn and directed by French animator Sylvain Chomet, with an all-star cast featuring Rihanna and Robert Pattinson, it centres on the fashion designer Christian Dior’s friendship with film star Marlene Dietrich.

Commenters praised its authentic visual appearance, while a behind the scenes page was published on Dior’s website highlighting the actors and design sketches, warding off accusations of AI-generation.

Despite this, some viewers believed that Dior’s advert showed several hallmarks of AI. A telltale sign of AI-generated content is garbled hands and fingers. Some viewers pointed to what they perceived as missing fingers and strange hand transitions in the advert.

In an interview with Variety, Chomet and producer Aton Soumache insisted that the advert was hand-drawn and generative AI was never used. But they have confirmed using a process known as “automated interpolation” to generate intermediate frames as “a very small part of the process” for the “repetitive, mechanical part of animation, not the creative work”. Automated interpolation is a standard digital animation tool that precedes AI, but now often involves its use.

The Dior case is illustrative of how vigilant audiences have become about AI use. Just as the presence of deepfakes risks undermining our trust in all images online, a few undisclosed AI-produced adverts can lead to scepticism of all advertising as viewers hunt for evidence of brands cutting corners rather than hiring creatives.
Even when specific accusations prove unfounded, the broader shift in advertising toward undisclosed generative AI raises deeper ethical and aesthetic questions for the industry as a whole.
AI models are often trained on artists’ work without compensation and threaten to put them out of work – not to mention AI datacentres’ impact on communities and the environment.

There’s also an irony in major brands baulking at the tedious task of getting the details right, and giving a misleading impression of fully human creation. These moral defects can diminish our aesthetic experience of AI adverts.

But putting aside morality, the revelation of AI use renders ads aesthetically worse in another way. Philosophers of art argue that forgeries are worse as artworks because they misrepresent achievement. We usually appreciate what the artist did in creating a work. So when we learn that a painting is not a genuine Vermeer, but a 20th century forgery by Van Meegeren, we judge it differently. (One philosopher even likens this betrayal to sexual infidelity – perhaps a bit much!)

Similarly, when we discover a beautiful, animated Christmas ad was produced with AI, we might lose appreciation for its creative process. The appearance of delicately hand-animated characters is a façade, generated not by artistic imagination but raw computational power. It’s not fraud, but it diminishes the experience.

Using AI to assist in creating complex scenery isn’t easy, and there can be skill to its use – some philosophers liken it to gardening. But it’s not the real process of hand-drawing and animation. To present it as such is a misrepresentation of achievement, imitating a style without the requisite labour behind it.

In response to these quandaries, some brands have taken to detailing the human processes behind their animated Christmas ads. Prada’s campaign emphasises traditional hand-drawn animation, with a separate behind-the-scenes video highlighting its artists. Others have followed suit. Barbour and Thatchers Cider each employed Aardman (producers of Wallace & Gromit) to hand-animate their adverts, while Etsy’s festive campaign is not-so-subtly titled “celebrate being human”. There are also video game studios which have detailed their refusal to use generative AI.

The praise showered on these traditional productions proves that audiences still care deeply about craft. A season built on warmth and sincerity cannot be manufactured by an algorithm that has never felt either.
Alex Fisher has received research funding from the Society for Applied Philosophy, the Leverhulme Trust, the Aristotelian Society, and the Royal Institute of Philosophy.

articles.title: Expect to see fewer and smaller potatoes this Christmas – it’s the ‘worst harvest since 1950s’
articles.author: Robin Gowers, Senior Lecturer at the Writtle School of Agriculture, Animal and Environmental Sciences, Anglia Ruskin University
paras: Britain’s potato harvest this winter could be one of the smallest in decades.

This is partly down to the hot summer and a poor growing year. Potatoes have shallow roots and need steady moisture, so dry spells cut yield and size. Where farmers had stored water to regularly irrigate, crops fared better.

With 75% of England in drought in September, and Wales also affected by dry conditions, one model estimated that British potato yields would be 11% below average. It used the 2018 harvest as a guide. Some farmers reported a greater than 50% drop in how many potatoes they were harvesting.
Wholesale prices had already risen by more than 40% by early August. By September, big British buyers were reportedly paying more than £300 a tonne for potatoes.
The Food and Drink Federation has warned of the worst potato harvest since the 1950s.

Growers have warned supermarkets to expect smaller potatoes and tighter supplies this year, so shoppers may need to accept wider variation in size and quality. This is partly because other European countries, which often provide supplies to the UK, suffered the same hot summer, and this affected their crops, too.

But shoppers may not feel the full effect of higher wholesale prices this winter. Potatoes are more likely to become significantly more expensive next year. It is also worth noting that many supermarkets subsidise potato prices.

Lidl has announced that a 2kg bag will cost 9p in the week before Christmas. The supermarket says it is funding the low price itself, so this price tells shoppers nothing about what the crop costs to grow.
Supermarkets agree prices and volumes with farmers well in advance. Retailers may absorb some of the higher costs this year rather than risk losing customers to competitors.
The bigger question is whether British farmers will carry on planting Britain’s favourite vegetable in future, and what happens if more decide it is no longer worth the risk.
In 2025, the issue was too many potatoes heading for shops – the UK produced 5.5 million tonnes, 8.5% more than the year before. This caused prices paid to farmers to collapse.

By February 2026, top-quality maris piper potatoes were fetching about £180 a tonne on the open market, less than half the £400 of a year earlier. Contract prices for the following year were also weaker.
Growers did what economics predicts: they planted less. Analysts put this year’s area in Great Britain at around 101,000 hectares, well below the 117,500 recorded in 2020.
Then came the heat and drought.
Why can’t farmers cash in?

Higher prices should encourage farmers to plant more. But a price spike helps only those with potatoes to sell at open-market rates. Most crops are grown under contract, and growers who struggle to deliver the agreed tonnage or quality may miss out.
Some big buyers that normally rely on contracts are buying open-market potatoes as fast as they can, so growers with uncommitted crops may do well.
Meanwhile, costs for farmers keep climbing. Conflict in the Middle East has pushed up energy and fertiliser costs. Labour and machinery are also more expensive.

Meanwhile, the end of the basic payment scheme (an annual payment for farmers that followed environmental guidelines) and controversies about its replacements may have removed a financial cushion that once helped farms through bad years.

The potato contract price is fixed in advance, so growers have little room to pass costs on. Tighter margins are also hitting buyers, packers and processors, but it is growers that carry the bulk of the weather risk.

Economists call this pattern the cobweb cycle. In the textbook version, farmers plant according to last season’s price, so a glut leads to a price crash, then cuts in planting, then shortage and high prices, then over-planting again. Potatoes have followed this familiar cycle almost to the letter this year.

Yet several forces pull the other way. Speaking before the summer’s hot weather and drought, in May, Scott Walker, chief executive of the industry body representing the potato sector, GB Potatoes, said that many growers were weighing up how much exposure they would carry into 2027. The body has warned that growers could leave the business or reduce their crop.

Contract prices were weaker this year, costs are higher, and drought has shown how exposed the crop is. Depressed cereal markets offer little alternative income, so a wholesale exit is not certain either.
Farmers will be looking closely at what supermarkets offer them in 2027. High open market prices alone will not bring growers back.

Two things matter most: the contracts offered this winter, and whether farmers can secure water supplies for next summer. Signs are that water access may remain tight. For instance, the Environment Agency put England’s reservoirs at only 54% of capacity in early October. Higher prices could prompt a rebound in planting, but a normal-weather harvest could tip the market back into glut, forcing prices down again.
Will British farmers stop planting potatoes?

In September 2026, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs saw no indication that winter supplies were at risk but added that it was too early to assess the drought’s full impact on potato production and that there was, at that point, no indication that winter potato supplies were at risk. Registered potato farmer numbers fell from about 2,466 in 2000 to 1,611 in 2020, when the statutory body collating data on potato farmers was discontinued. But each bad year pushes more to ask whether the crop is worth it.

Tim Rooke, National Farmers’ Union potato policy group chair, said in 2025 that the UK imports approximately 1 million tonnes of frozen chips a year, because the risk against return on investment of growing potatoes is astronomically high.

A food system that leaves a shrinking number of growers to absorb the weather and price risk should not be surprised when they plant less. One option could be fairer contracts that share risk, and investment in water storage. But less certain supply chains and more volatile prices could cost shoppers more.
Climate change means water shortages and high temperatures will happen more often across Europe. Potato farmers are, therefore, likely to face these challenges more regularly in the future.

articles.title: The UK shouldn’t worry about taxing big companies that threaten to leave
articles.author: Alan Collins, Professor Emeritus in Economics and Public Policy, Nottingham Trent University
paras: There are huge companies making vast amounts of money in the UK. And some of those firms pay very little tax on the money they make.

This makes some people angry. It seems unfair, after all, that a company the size of Starbucks – worth over US$100 billion (£75 billion) – paid no corporation tax in the UK last year. Or the year before that.

Research suggests that some companies manage to do this by using a variety of clever strategies (not readily available to smaller firms) that help them to legally shift profits out of countries with higher tax rates to countries with lower tax rates.
In theory, each of these complex arrangements could be forensically examined by the UK’s tax authorities.
But doing so in practice would be a considerable burden in terms of scrutiny and enforcement. There could also be time-consuming appeals processes and legal challenges.
An international approach is also problematic. One country imposing a tax on global profits raises difficulties for tax authorities in confirming the veracity of international declared accounts.
But if the UK really wanted to do something about international firms paying zero (or nearly zero) corporation tax, there are options.
What if, for example, the tax authority charged Starbucks a flat, minimum level of corporation tax per outlet based on what comparable domestic businesses in the area pay?
If Starbucks chose to close stores rather than pay up, this would be fine.

The coffee shop market is a popular one, or in economic terms, “highly contestable”. So if Starbucks decided to abandon its branch on your local high street, another coffee shop – let’s call it “Moonpounds” – is likely to step in.
And while there may be dedicated fans of Starbucks coffee, there are others who are not, and who would happily spend their money at other coffee chains, or indeed independent coffee shops.
Moonpounds would retain jobs and contribute more effectively to the local economy and tax base – and not channel profits abroad.

The idea here is that whether or not a particular multinational corporation continues operating in the country should be of no interest to the tax authority, which should respond to threats with a shrug. It’s an approach to taxation one might term “existential indifference”.

Under a principle of existential indifference, threats of ceasing trading should be ignored. Similarly, impassioned defences based on job losses and VAT receipts to the exchequer should be ignored as jobs and VAT receipts would also be provided by new market entrants.

This means that there are many potential new entrant businesses that could easily replace a given Starbucks cafe if it closed. They would routinely be contributing more to the vibrancy of the local economy and the UK exchequer.
The same theory applies to many other big businesses.

Delivering items to people’s homes is another highly contestable market. And there are plenty of tech companies that would be happy to help with your internet searches. The same goes for cloud data storage or app sales.
For many of these services provided by large companies, there are plenty of potential new entrants and competitors who would be happy to take over.

The idea of pushing taxes on big firms who employ lots of people can sometimes be seen as anti-business or anti-growth. But the idea of fairness in the corporate world was something that past economic thinkers encouraged.

In the 18th century, for example, Adam Smith, the “father of economics”, was not an advocate of taxing profits. Yet he was also not in favour of tax outcomes causing persistent income or revenue inequality.

In the 20th century, John Maynard Keynes primarily viewed corporation tax as just one lever of fiscal policy to be increased or decreased depending on the stage of the economic cycle. He also viewed taxation as an appropriate response to excess profits.

Economic thought on taxing the profits of big international companies has now evolved to the position where even the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) actively promotes a minimum corporation tax rate (15%) to stop multinational companies from shifting profits to low-tax havens and to try to obstruct the competitive lowering (or race to the bottom) of tax rates among countries.

The OECD appears to support the idea that effective and fairer corporation taxes can be designed with sufficient political will. And that political will should not be weakened by the worry that some international firms will leave along the way.

Alan Collins has previously received funding from various grant providing bodies including the Economic and Social Research Council, Engineering and Physical Science Research Council and the European Commission. He is a very passive member of the Labour Party.

articles.title: Cop31 climate summit debates how fossil fuel subsidies have hidden costs on nature
articles.author: Benjamin Selwyn, Professor of International Relations and International Development, Department of International Relations, University of Sussex
paras: As world leaders gather at the UN climate summit, Cop31, in Turkey, one issue has returned to the centre of climate politics: subsidies. Brazil has renewed calls for countries to phase out fossil-fuel subsidies, while campaigners and several governments argue that public money should no longer support industries driving climate change.

The debate is usually framed quite simply. Governments spend billions reducing the cost of producing or consuming coal, oil and gas. Remove those subsidies, and the transition to cleaner energy will accelerate.
But this focus on visible subsidies obscures a much larger one.

More than 70 years ago, the political economist Karl William Kapp argued that modern economies depend on a vast invisible subsidy – the systematic transfer of social and environmental costs onto society and nature.

Published in 1950, his book The Social Costs of the Business Enterprise argued that environmental degradation, public health harms and resource depletion are not merely unfortunate by-products of economic growth. Rather, they are inseparable from a market system organised around private profit and competitive cost reduction.

Mainstream economics describes such harms as “externalities” that arise when markets fail to reflect all relevant costs. Kapp, by contrast, argued that pollution, ecological degradation and ill health were recurring outcomes of an economic system in which market prices systematically exclude many of the real costs of production.

Kapp’s argument was that the market mechanism itself rewards economic activities that can offload part of their costs onto workers, communities, public budgets and ecosystems. Cost-shifting is not the exception but a foundational means through which competitive market economies reproduce themselves.

From this perspective, subsidies extend beyond tax breaks, preferential loans and direct government support. The deeper subsidy arises when economic activity proceeds without accounting for its full social and ecological costs.

The climate crisis provides an obvious example. Fossil fuels appear relatively cheap because many of their costs, including air pollution, ecological degradation and climate disruption, are borne elsewhere.
Recent attempts to place monetary values on environmental damage, although developed for very different purposes, lend support to Kapp’s argument.

Paradoxically, many of these initiatives were designed to integrate nature more fully into economic calculation and investment decisions, yet their findings reveal the extent to which profitability depends on costs that remain outside market accounts.

One 2024 industry report found that the environmental costs associated with cereal-grain cultivation in eastern Asia were almost three times greater than the revenues generated by the sector. Similar patterns appeared across crop cultivation in southern Asia and South America. In many cases, environmental damages exceeded revenues. This indicates that if these costs were fully borne within production, many companies in this part of the agricultural economy could not remain economically viable.
Comparable dynamics are visible across mining, chemicals and cement production, where estimated environmental damages also exceeded revenues.

The same pattern is, unsurprisingly, evident in fossil fuels. According to an International Monetary Fund estimate, the global underpricing of fossil fuels amounts to an industrial subsidy of roughly US$6.7 trillion (£5 trillion) annually. This figure includes climate damages, air pollution and other costs excluded from market prices. Rather than appearing on balance sheets, they are dispersed across societies and ecosystems.
The apparent profitability of major sectors of the global economy depends not simply on technological innovation or productive efficiency, but on the continuing ability to transfer costs elsewhere.

This reveals a contradiction at the heart of contemporary climate policy. At Cop31, governments are debating how to eliminate environmentally harmful subsidies while simultaneously encouraging private investment in the green transition. Yet both discussions often assume that markets merely require better incentives and more accurate pricing to align profit with sustainability.

Kapp argued that environmental destruction persists not because costs are poorly measured, but because economic success depends on excluding them from market calculations by shifting them onto society and nature.
Recalculating nature costs
The Cop31 debate over subsidies is important. It is right that social movements and progressive governments push for, and commit to, more renewable energy generation.

But it should also encourage climate-conscious people to think beyond subsidies that appear in government budgets. The larger question is whether an economy can genuinely be considered sustainable when many its costs are systematically transferred onto others.

Seventy-five years after Kapp first made the argument, climate breakdown, biodiversity loss and ecological instability suggest that the hidden subsidy to capital that he identified has become one of the defining features of this era.

The challenge is not only to remove public support from environmentally destructive activities while increasing investment in renewables. It is also to confront an economic system that treats society and nature as repositories for costs that markets refuse to count.

Benjamin Selwyn does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Americans are eating way less turkey than we used to
articles.author: Jay L. Zagorsky, Associate Professor of Business, Boston University
paras: One of the most quintessential American things is having roasted turkey on the table at a Thanksgiving feast. While that remains the norm, Americans are eating much less of this kind of poultry today than in the past. Annual consumption has fallen by more than 25% over the past three decades, while demand for chicken has soared.

I’m a business school professor who has written about the economics of various holidays. I find turkeys fascinating, because even though I live in an urban area, a large group of wild turkeys has taken over my backyard.
And I can offer several good explanations for the turkey slump.
Receding since the late 1990s
Domesticated turkeys, unlike their wild cousins, are a big business.
More than US$5 billion worth of the birds were sold in 2025. That’s no chicken feed.

However, it’s the latest sign of the industry’s decline. U.S. consumers are drifting away from eating turkey. Back in 1995, the average American consumed 17.7 pounds (8 kilograms) of turkey each year. By 2025, consumption had fallen to just 13.2 pounds (6 kg).

While turkey consumption started to recede in the late 1990s, it began accelerating around 2008, when the Great Recession was underway. Occasionally, turkey production ticks upward a little, as happened in 2026 as demand for niche products like turkey jerky rose, but the long-term picture is one of steady decline.

It’s not like Americans are eating less poultry overall. Chicken consumption has steadily grown during this turkey slump, rising about 50% from 69 pounds (31 kg) in 1995 to 104 pounds (47 kg) in 2025.
In other words, we’re eating almost eight times more chicken than turkey. Well, at least the 95% of Americans who aren’t vegetarian or vegan are.
More costly at every step in the supply chain
Government agencies, researchers and some pundits have identified two possible explanations for why Americans are eating less turkey.
First: pocketbook concerns. Turkey often costs more than chicken, except when it goes on sale just before Thanksgiving.

Over the past 25 years, wholesale turkey prices per pound averaged about 10% higher than chicken, according to U.S. Department of Agriculture data. That price, which is what big retailers typically pay, affects what you owe at checkout.

For example, just before the 2026 Thanksgiving sales began, a Bell & Evans fresh whole turkey was going for $4.99 a pound, while a Bell & Evans fresh whole chicken cost $3.49 a pound at my local supermarket. That’s $1.50 a pound difference, which is significant in an economy where many people feel economically pinched.
Nationally, you will see similar price differences, with fresh turkey being more expensive than fresh chicken.
So, why is turkey pricier than chicken?
Both turkeys and chickens are fed a diet of corn and soybeans. However, turkeys consume a higher percentage of soybeans. And soybeans currently cost about twice as much as corn.
The latest data shows turkey feed costs are up almost 80%, without accounting for inflation, since 2000, while chicken feed costs have climbed only 60%.
The second reason has to do with the size of today’s families.
The typical Bell & Evans whole chicken my grocery store sells weighs approximately 4 pounds, while its fresh turkeys tend to range between 10 and 12 pounds.

Big birds are handy if you have a lot of mouths to feed, but American families have shrunk over time. Today the average household includes only 2.5 people. The extra half-person does not represent children who are picky eaters or people who don’t like eating meat. It just means the typical family has between two and three people.
That means cooking a 10-pound turkey results in 4 pounds of food per person, which is far more than almost anyone who is not a competitive food eater can consume.

Cooking a 4-pound chicken, however, results in a more manageable 1.2 pounds of poultry per eater after getting rid of the bones, which make up about a quarter of a chicken. In simple terms, buying a whole chicken often results in one or two meals per person. Cooking a whole turkey often yields enough meat to produce meals for an entire week.

There are two more factors to consider. First, a 10-pound turkey costs a lot more than a 4-pound chicken. A 10-pound fresh bird at $4.99 a pound sets you back almost $50, while a $3.49-per-pound chicken that weighs 4 pounds costs under $14.

Last, bigger birds take longer to roast. Cooking a 10-pound turkey in an oven takes about three hours, while a 4-pound chicken takes about two. That extra hour is a big burden in an increasingly time-pressed society.
In case you were wondering, the world record for eating a turkey is held by Joey Chestnut. He gobbled down 9.35 pounds of turkey off the bone in 10 minutes in 2014. Please do not try that at home.
If you need to save money on turkey this holiday season, you should consider buying a frozen one. They are much cheaper.
But can you save even more by going turkey hunting?
Given all the large wild turkeys roosting in my backyard, I looked into what it would take. I live in Massachusetts, where hunting wild turkeys before Thanksgiving is legal.

For much of the fall, hunters are allowed to use only bows and arrows. Beyond needing to be a proficient archer, they also have to purchase a sporting license, a turkey permit and an archery stamp for $95 each year.
Having learned about that, I’m sticking to buying my turkeys in the supermarket.

Jay L. Zagorsky does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: What does an ‘AI-generated’ label in advertising actually tell us?
articles.author: Denitsa Dineva, Reader (Associate Professor) in Marketing, Cardiff University
paras: Advertising is about persuasion. It exists to sell products and lifestyles, ideas and stories.
And while people have become pretty good at treating adverts with a degree of scepticism, artificial intelligence (AI) has added another layer of uncertainty.
When we see an advert labelled “AI-generated” on social media or anywhere else online, we know that AI was involved in making it. What we usually don’t know is how.

AI may, for example, have been one tool in a largely human-led creative process, used to edit an image or refine text. Or it might have generated much of the finished advert with limited human input. A simple “AI-generated” label can encompass both extremes and everything in between.
The distinction matters because AI can change how consumers react to advertising. There is evidence that disclosing AI involvement can reduce levels of trust.
Other research points to some overall resistance to AI from consumers, although reactions vary considerably depending on what the technology is being used to create.

Disclosure itself is nothing new in advertising. When influencers use “#ad” on social media, or labels pointing to “sponsored content”, disclosures help consumers recognise the commercial side of what they are watching or reading.
Our research, however, indicates that AI disclosures serve a different purpose.

For while traditional advertising disclosures tell consumers something about why content is being shown to them, AI disclosure labels instead draw attention to how it was produced. But they do not necessarily reveal the respective roles of humans and machines.
For decades, advertisers have used digital tools to alter content. A designer might retouch a photograph for example, or remove a background while retaining control over the creative decisions.

AI blurs the distinction between editing existing content and creating new content because it can generate elements of that content by itself. A person may still develop the idea and refine the result, but the balance between human and machine contribution can vary considerably.

Disclosing that AI was involved can then invite judgments about who or what created the content, how much human input was involved, and whether the use of AI was appropriate. This may also help explain criticism of AI-led campaigns by brands such as Coca-Cola and Gucci.
Governments and platforms are beginning to address these questions through new approaches to AI transparency.

The EU wants to make sure that providers of certain generative AI systems are subjected to strict requirements about disclosure. Meanwhile, technology is emerging that allows digital content, including adverts, to carry accessible information about its provenance and editing history.

And the detail matters. Meta acknowledged that its “Made with AI” label appeared on content involving only minor AI modifications and did not provide sufficient context. It replaced the “Made with AI” wording with “AI info” and later made the label less prominent when AI had been used to edit, rather than generate, content.
We are also seeing the same kind of ambiguity appearing in reverse. Labels with the words “human-made” and “no AI” are emerging to signal human authorship.
But do these mean no AI whatsoever, or a predominantly human process in which AI played a supporting role? Both kinds of label can obscure as much as they reveal.

For the time being, then, consumers should take a little time to consider how they interpret AI labels. The term “AI-generated” tells us something – but not everything – about how content was produced. It does not, by itself, mean the result is fake, poor quality or untrustworthy.
Nor will it spell out the human role – who developed the idea, selected and refined the output, checked its accuracy and decided what ultimately appeared.

Ultimately, an AI label should be a starting point for evaluating content, rather than the end. “AI-generated” tells us that AI played a role, but understanding how it was used and how much human judgement shaped the result would tell us far more.

articles.title: Debate in New York City over city-run groceries is not just about food, but something bigger
articles.author: Nevin Cohen, Professor, Graduate School of Public Health and Health Policy, City University of New York
paras: New York City is moving closer to launching its effort to counter food inflation by opening five city-run grocery stores. Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced in May 2026 that the first store would open in the Hunts Point neighborhood of the South Bronx in 2027, with another in East Harlem to follow.

Five stores, one in each borough, are unlikely to substantially change grocery prices in a city with nearly 1,000 supermarkets and more than 8 million inhabitants. But each could make a meaningful difference to the grocery bills of local shoppers by selling essentials at below-market prices.

Even with just five planned stores set to open in lower-income neighborhoods, the initiative has ignited fierce opposition from independent grocers, supermarket trade associations and a coalition representing immigrant-owned food businesses.
What explains this pushback?

As a food policy scholar, I believe this opposition is about more than the immediate economic impact of five stores. It is about the precedent they could establish. Mamdani’s initiative challenges an entrenched expectation that the government should leave the provision of consumer goods to private enterprise even as it encourages businesses to invest in certain locations, regulates their activities and helps low-income shoppers through various food assistance programs.

The reality is more complicated. For at least a century, New York’s food economy has not operated independently of government. In fact, public policies and investments have long shaped where supermarkets open, which businesses can operate with a profit, and how residents obtain food.
It’s just that they have done so in ways consumers often don’t see.

That is why the five grocery stores carry a broader significance, in my view. They offer a different model of public investment that makes the government much more visible in providing an essential service – and more accountable for its results. New Yorkers will get an opportunity to judge that contribution directly.
If the stores succeed, they may change not just what people expect to pay for groceries, but what they expect their city government to provide.
New York City has committed US$70 million to develop these stores, which will be open to all.
While they will be managed by private operators, the city will provide rent-free space, prioritize publicly owned sites and ensure that essential foods are priced 30% below typical retail prices.
In this respect, the stores offer a “public option” – a government-provided good or service that exists alongside private alternatives, like public schools and city hospitals.

Municipal grocery stores would offer New Yorkers a similar choice alongside private retailers. But as a public option, they would create a visible alternative against which shoppers can judge privately owned stores, setting a benchmark for food prices and service quality. They would also demonstrate how public investment can be used to make an essential good more affordable.
At his May announcement, Mamdani described the proposed Bronx store and its surrounding development as “physical proof of our conviction that government can be a force for good.”
A fresh form of intervention
Government-supported food retailing has a long history in New York City despite opposition by existing businesses.

In 1934, Mayor Fiorello La Guardia’s administration began selling discounted milk to low-income families, but the initiative drew complaints from grocers about unfair competition. Independent merchants similarly protested the city’s efforts to subsidize a new Pathmark supermarket in East Harlem in the 1990s, warning that it would put local grocers out of business.

A more recent example is the city’s Food Retail Expansion to Support Health program, known as FRESH. Since 2009, it has offered supermarket developers and operators long-term tax breaks and zoning incentives to build or expand dozens of stores in underserved neighborhoods.
These incentives have helped increase grocery retail space, but shoppers don’t see the public support behind them.

FRESH is just one example of an approach toward supermarket financing that gained momentum in the 1990s, when governments sought to address social problems by encouraging private investment. Food insecurity was blamed on a scarcity of neighborhood supermarkets, not on prices being beyond reach for local shoppers.

Subsidizing new stores promised better nutrition and economic development without confronting poverty or inequality, and FRESH reflects that approach. Participating supermarkets must devote space to perishable foods, but they’re not required to offer affordable prices. That may be one reason why researchers have found that adding supermarkets to low-income neighborhoods, by itself, doesn’t substantially improve residents’ diets.

This hidden government role is hardly confined to grocery stores. Much of what government does for Americans is delivered indirectly, through tax credits, subsidies and private institutions. Because the public contribution is obscured, people often give credit to private markets for the benefits provided by public policy, from student loans to healthcare.
This invisibility is a consequence of policy design and influences how citizens understand government, a phenomenon that political scientist Suzanne Mettler described as “the submerged state.”
Bringing the state into the open
Municipal grocery stores depart from the traditional model in two important ways.

First, they make affordability an explicit condition of public investment rather than the outcome of increased retail competition. Second, they make government’s contribution visible. For example, the stores will share distinct branding so shoppers know who’s responsible for the affordable food.

If the stores deliver reliable savings, shoppers may begin to see affordable food as something government can help provide, not an outcome determined entirely by private markets. When public benefits are obscured, people are more likely to underestimate government’s contribution to their lives. Visible programs, like a physical store in the neighborhood, make that contribution easier to notice and evaluate.

Visibility also creates accountability. A customer at a private supermarket that received a tax break to expand isn’t likely to tie the store’s prices or food quality to government policy. At a municipal grocery store, with clear branding, the connection is unmistakable.

To be sure, critics’ concerns deserve serious attention. Many independent grocery stores are owned by immigrant entrepreneurs operating on thin margins. Groups representing bodegas and independent supermarkets warn that a publicly subsidized competitor could draw away their customers. Some may lose business.

Yet East Harlem’s Pathmark demonstrates that new supermarkets and smaller retailers can coexist. Between 2000 and 2015, the number of small grocery stores and bodegas in the neighborhood increased from 100 to 126, while supermarkets rose from 10 to 18. That said, those figures don’t establish Pathmark’s effects on individual businesses.

The municipal stores’ impact on nearby retailers remains an open question. But the task for New York City is to ensure that private operators deliver excellent service and real savings, and that their commercial interests don’t undermine the public mission. It will also need to provide good working conditions and track effects on nearby businesses.
Ultimately, public ownership doesn’t guarantee success. But it makes government’s responsibility for the outcome impossible to miss.
Nevin Cohen receives research funding from the City of New York.

articles.title: The Microsoft outage is an urgent wake-up call for greater digital resilience
articles.author: A.R.E. Taylor, Senior Lecturer in Communications, University of Exeter
paras: Friday the 13th turned out to be very unlucky indeed for Microsoft. A major outage of the tech giant’s services put a halt to digital communication for millions across the world.
So after UK government warnings to prepare for a possible cyber-attack, perhaps the bigger threat to the online world is simply the fragile design of internet infrastructure.
That fragility was plain to see on November 13. Emails and video calls stopped working as Microsoft struggled to fix “connectivity problems”.
The crash caused massive disruption to public services including hospitals and schools.

At the time of writing, what caused the outage remains unclear. But whatever it was also highlights the risks of market concentration, where a relatively small number of powerful corporations have become responsible for providing and maintaining most of the digital services on which we depend.
Microsoft has previously presented that dominance as a corporate strength. The company once claimed that serving billions of customers gives their global digital ecosystem a “unique vantage point”.
But while this level of market domination is good for business, it is not necessarily good for infrastructural resilience.

The internet has become increasingly dominated by a relatively small number of powerful corporations. The expansion of cloud computing has accelerated this centralisation, concentrating the provision of computing resources in the hands of a few major companies.
As Friday 13th demonstrated, this level of concentration can lead to widespread disruption.
And it’s not even an isolated incident.

A similar outage revealed similar risks in July 2024 when a faulty security update crashed millions of systems that used Microsoft Windows. IT systems around the world suddenly ground to a halt, leaving pharmacies, airports and banks unable to operate.

Just last month, on October 22, AI testing revealed security vulnerabilities in a programme which underpinned roughly 70% of the world’s websites. Governments and businesses took thousands of sites and online services offline to prevent potential cyber-attacks and data theft.
A month before that, autonomous AI agents developed by OpenAI hacked government infrastructure.
So there are clearly weaknesses in the current design of the internet and its enormously complex ecosystem of interdependencies.
Those ecosystems are not just chips and wires. It can be easy to forget the people who deliver the digital services we often take for granted.

The internet depends upon extensive material infrastructure and the operation of that infrastructure is not automatic. It relies on a large human workforce, which operates amid demanding schedules, tight deadlines and the pressure to maintain uninterruptible services.
As an anthropologist who conducts fieldwork in the data centre industry, I have spent a lot of time with the people who work behind the screens of the digital world.
Where organisations are understaffed or place excessive demands on their employees, the capacity to undertake comprehensive testing, monitoring and diagnostic work may be compromised.

The burden of restoring services following the Microsoft outage will fall heavily on IT professionals across the affected organisations. Many of them will be required to work demanding hours to bring the disrupted systems back online.
The physical and psychological toll that major infrastructure failures can impose on these workers remains an important dimension of the wider costs of digital disruption.
All eggs inside one digital basket

And then there’s the social cost. Sociologists of risk have long argued that the vulnerabilities of technologically advanced societies stem, in part, from their growing dependence on complex and interconnected infrastructures.
The consolidation of digital infrastructure has concentrated considerable power and responsibility in the hands of a relatively small number of private corporations.
And the Microsoft incident illustrates the extent to which organisations have come to place their operational continuity in the hands of major technology providers.
Microsoft’s infrastructure underpins an enormous range of everyday activities – activities undertaken by schools and hospitals, by businesses and charities.

When these services become unavailable, the consequences extend far beyond the immediate inconvenience of being unable to access an email account. Organisations, vital public services and even nation states which outsource essential aspects of their digital operations to a single provider can find themselves unable to function when that provider experiences a major failure.
The growing dependence on a concentrated technology ecosystem therefore raises fundamental questions about digital resilience.
As societies become increasingly reliant on online services, the consequences of infrastructure failures could become more extensive – and more damaging.

articles.title: In a world of anti-environment backlash, Andy Burnham walks a line between popular and green
articles.author: Renaud Foucart, Senior Lecturer in Economics, Lancaster University Management School, Lancaster University
paras: Andy Burnham took to the floor at the UN climate summit, Cop31, in Turkey and promised a “new era of British leadership”.

The UK’s new prime minister does not talk a lot about the environment, and many of his recent decisions have disappointed environmental activists. Since late October, he has approved a new gas field in the North Sea. He decided to extend the freeze on fuel duty, and has floated reducing the electric vehicle target.

His government also recently reduced support for heat pumps. And his chancellor, John Healey, has recently said the government backs Heathrow airport’s project to build a third runway. Although some sources are reporting that Burnham has still not confirmed it.
Yet Burnham might end up being the saviour of Britain’s ambitious net zero agenda, the initiative to push countries to remove as much greenhouse gas as they emit by 2050.

His plan has a razor-sharp focus on consumers, and a by-product of this might be to cut fossil fuel use too. But along the way, he looks like he is ready to drop any decision that could make the broader agenda unpopular.

Just six months ago, the country looked like it might be on track for a Nigel Farage-led Reform right-wing populist government. Reform was well ahead of Labour and the Conservatives in the polls. And Farage does not hide his intention to scrap net zero targets if he ever gets into power.
Today, Labour is pulling further ahead in the polls. It would be useful to take seriously how Andy Burnham got there.
There are broadly three ways to promote environmental policy. One is de-growth: the idea that we can only save the planet by doing less.

Another is boosterism, the spirit behind Boris Johnson’s net zero idea. It promises a green revolution that unleashes decades of growth from new technologies. This works as a vision, but there can be a backlash when people face the short-term costs.
Then there is Andy Burnham’s: the consumer-first environmental agenda.
Why it might boost electricity use

Take the current electric vehicle target, that 80% of new cars sold in the UK must be electric by 2030. It looks like Burnham is happy to lower it if it can protect consumers from higher costs. But, so far, Britain has also chosen not to tax cheap Chinese car imports, unlike the European Union and the United States.
But around a third of Chinese imports are electric vehicles. So, this could push up EV use significantly.

The approval of the Jackdaw gas field, 150 miles off the Scottish coast, follows the same ruthless logic. Extracting gas domestically is not unambiguously bad for the environment. One argument is that if Britain does not exploit that field, it may end up importing even more polluting foreign gas instead. Although the benefits could be minimal.

Gas is traded globally, so Jackdaw will not affect global prices. But it will raise money for the government’s energy wealth fund. This will be spent on renewable investment and lower electricity bills.

Sometimes, supporting consumers also supports the environment. Cutting value added tax and green charges on electricity bills could encourage people to switch from gas boilers and petrol cars to heat pumps and electric vehicles.

This benefits the planet but also should make electricity cheaper for everyone down the line. A big driver of high electricity costs in Britain is the lack of demand: the cost of infrastructure is shared among too few consumers.

But, sometimes, supporting consumers means making decisions that totally conflict with the general goal. Take the decision to freeze fuel duty, which has appeared in every budget since 2011. Protecting consumers from higher petrol prices discourages people from switching to electric vehicles. That makes electricity more expensive for everyone. And it has cost the Treasury £139 billion so far.

However, motorists are way too dangerous to anger. Emmanuel Macron spent his two terms in France under the permanent threat of the yellow vest riots. The movement started with a complaint about petrol prices and speed limits.
So Burnham chooses not to anger them.

Then there’s the proposed plan to build a third runway at Heathrow. Burnham, a champion of decentralisation, has never been a fan of the London-centred project. But it appears that he may (or may not) now back it. Certainly his chancellor thinks so.
To understand why, it can be useful to look at the project impact assessment. Expanding Heathrow would potentially be bad for the environment and good for the economy.
The project is expected to bring passengers more than £20 billion in direct economic benefits, and cheaper airfares.

Current congestion at Heathrow means airlines can charge very high prices, for instance during school holidays. So a third runway could open up competition, and bring fares down. So it looks like Burnham may be willing to cut part of his environmental goals to let Britons afford some cheaper trips abroad.
But, overall, it is unclear how much of his broader political agenda Burnham must sacrifice for social acceptability. He must also try and balance this with encouraging investment in Britain.

With anti-environmental populism on the rise around the world, Burnham’s current popularity is based on getting this balance right. If he can, it might be a sign he could quietly deliver a new era of British leadership, and a stealthy boost for the environment.

articles.title: The 2% tax hike on rental income is bad for landlords and tenants alike. Here’s what reform looks like
articles.author: Emma Laurie, Emerita Fellow, University of Southampton
paras: The October budget brought unwelcome news for private landlords in England, Wales and Northern Ireland. From April 2027, they will pay a further 2% tax on rental income, in addition to the 2% increase announced in the 2025 budget.

Given the notoriously high cost of private renting in the UK, there may be little sympathy for landlords. And the new tax rise will most likely be passed on to tenants through rent increases anyway – a view shared by both the National Residential Landlords Association and the UK’s public finance watchdog.

I’m a law professor specialising in social and private rental markets. I believe that the new tax represents a major missed opportunity. Instead of increasing landlords’ tax burden – and indirectly raising rents for tenants – the government could have taken the chance to negotiate with landlords to cap rent increases.
But given that the new tax will probably be passed on to renters, how much power do tenants themselves have to resist rent hikes?
The Renters’ Rights Act 2025 was rightly hailed as a landmark change in tenants’ rights. It abolished the notorious section 21 “no fault” eviction, effective as of May 1, 2026.

But the act is very unlikely to protect tenants from a rent increase that is in line with the going rate. Landlords can only give notice to raise the rent once a year, and must provide a minimum of two months’ notice. Tenants can challenge an increase by applying to a tribunal, but they will only be successful if the new rent is more expensive than the local market rate.

Both tenants and landlords are encouraged to provide information about rents for other similar properties. There is no single approved source for such information, but websites such as Zoopla and Rightmove are typically used.

Before applying to the tribunal, it is sensible to try to reach agreement over the rent. The 2025 act does give tenants much greater flexibility. They can now end a tenancy with two months’ notice, whereas before the act, tenancies would often have a defined duration, for example 12 months. This means that tenants are no longer tied to paying for a tenancy that has become unaffordable. It may also make landlords more willing to negotiate to keep good tenants.
But the broader point remains: the 2025 act cannot protect against rent increases in areas where demand outstrips supply.

When the Renters’ Rights Act was going through Parliament, the government was adamant that rent caps would not be introduced. At the time, I argued that it was part of an unspoken deal to win landlords’ support for abolishing section 21 evictions.
How the government can protect renters

Rent controls are a source of controversy in the UK, largely because of the legacy of measures in force for most of the 20th century. But since rents were brought out of control by Margaret Thatcher’s government in 1988, the private rental sector has adopted a classically neoliberal approach.

There is no universally agreed definition of neoliberalism. In housing, it generally means that private landlords should be free to charge market rents for homes that offer relatively little stability.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has recently recognised that the neoliberal model “simply doesn’t work well enough for ordinary people”. What, then, is the alternative?

Instead of imposing the additional 2% tax on landlords, the government could have taken a first step to making renting more affordable by getting landlord support to cap rent increases. In other words, a trade-off between tax income, benefiting the government, and rent capping, which would potentially benefit tenants.
Rent control measures have become increasingly sophisticated, but they are certainly not a silver bullet for the housing crisis.

However, reducing landlords’ tax obligations in exchange for modest price capping – for example by tying rises to the Consumer Prices Index, as Scotland has done – could work for landlords and renters alike.

Landlords have long expressed dissatisfaction with the numerous changes to their tax position since 2015. They do have a point: cumulative changes have made the English tax and regulation regime one of the least favourable in Europe and North America.

Any such deal would, of course, mean the government giving up the expected additional tax income – estimated at £35 million in 2027-28 and £445 million by 2030-31. But if the prime minister is serious about moving away from a rental housing market dominated by four decades of neoliberal thinking, this proposal would represent a modest first step in the right direction – one that would benefit everyone.

articles.title: From ancient Asia to the AI age: Has China’s ‘beauty stratagem’ found a new victim in Nvidia’s Jensen Huang?
articles.author: Linggong Kong, Ph.D. Candidate in Political Science, Auburn University
paras: Extramarital activities have led to the resignation of one of America’s most influential tech bosses, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The saga has also raised the specter of an age-old spying tactic: the “honey trap.”

Huang stepped down following media reports of an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, a Singapore-based executive suspected of having ties to Chinese intelligence agencies. She previously worked for Megaspeed, a cloud computing company under U.S. scrutiny for allegedly helping China obtain restricted AI chips.
Jensen Huang acknowledged an affair. And amid reports of a second with a company executive who reports to him, he tendered his resignation to the Nvidia board on Nov. 12, 2026.

The sensitivity of Huang’s work – AI is increasingly seen as central to national security – has turned a company matter into an international issue. China’s Foreign Ministry has denied the espionage allegations and accused the U.S. of “fabricating so-called spy narratives and ⁠⁠⁠⁠using them as a pretext for imposing ⁠⁠⁠⁠a technological blockade.” Nvidia says it has no reason to believe company secrets have been leaked.
Yet part of what makes the accusations so believable is history is dotted with examples of men being distracted, compromised or spied on by attractive men and women deployed for that purpose.
Indeed, in China it recalls an ancient political tactic known as “meiren ji” or the “beauty stratagem.”

As a scholar specializing in U.S.-China relations, I believe that regardless of the particulars of the Huang case, the political logic behind the beauty stratagem – using personal relationships to obtain information, influence decisions and weaken opponents – remains relevant today. As such, it would be no surprise if the tactic was being used amid the growing U.S.-China competition over AI and advanced semiconductors.
The beauty stratagem of Ancient China

“Meiren ji” is one of “Thirty-Six Stratagems,” a Chinese military text of uncertain origin but generally believed to have derived from oral and written histories from the Warring States period — 475–221 BCE. Its 31st stratagem states that personal relationships can be used to influence political opponents and recommends exploiting an adversary’s personal desires and emotional vulnerabilities to weaken their judgment and undermine their leadership.
The “Thirty-Six Stratagems” is both a playbook for warfare and a reflection on past experience.
Indeed, one of China’s most famous beauty stratagem stories dates back more than 2,000 years to the Spring and Autumn period of Chinese history.

In the fifth century BCE, King Goujian of Yue, in modern-day southern China, was defeated by King Fuchai of Wu, its northern neighbor, and forced to submit. But Goujian secretly rebuilt his strength and prepared for revenge.
According to the ancient historical text “Wu Yue Chun Qiu,” Yue sent two beautiful women – Xi Shi and Zheng Dan – to Fuchai, hoping he would become distracted by pleasure and neglect state affairs.
The plan reportedly worked. Fuchai, seemingly enchanted by the beautiful women, gradually ignored Yue’s threat. Meanwhile, Goujian prepared for war and in 473 BCE Yue conquered Wu.
Xi Shi’s actual role in Wu’s downfall remains unclear. Wu’s defeat involved poor political decisions and Yue’s military recovery.
Still, the story illustrated an important idea in Chinese political strategy: exploiting an opponent’s personal weaknesses can sometimes be more effective than confronting him directly.
A similar tactic appears in the 14th-century novel “Romance of the Three Kingdoms,” considered one of the classics of Chinese literature.

It tells the story of Dong Zhuo, a powerful warlord who controlled the imperial court during the late Eastern Han Dynasty. To remove him, Wang Yun, a senior court official loyal to the Han Dynasty promised a beautiful young woman, named Diaochan, in marriage to Dong Zhuo’s military commander. He then offered the same woman to Dong Zhuo.

The scheme fueled jealousy and distrust between the two men, eventually enabling Wang Yun to persuade Dong Zhuo’s underling to kill him. Wang Yun then briefly took charge of the imperial court on behalf of the Han emperor.
The ‘honey trap’ of modern spyware

In modern intelligence operations, using romantic or sexual relationships to approach targets, obtain sensitive information or exert influence is commonly called a “honey trap.” It is, moreover, certainly not unique to China. Western and Soviet intelligence agencies used intimate relationships for espionage frequently during the Cold War.

Modern China also has documented cases. One example involves French diplomat Bernard Boursicot and the Chinese opera performer Shi Pei Pu. The pair met in Beijing in 1964 and maintained a long-term intimate relationship. Throughout, Boursicot was providing French diplomatic documents to China. The spying was eventually exposed and both involved were prosecuted for espionage in France in the 1980s.

A more recent example involves former U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell and Christine Fang, a suspected Chinese intelligence operative. Swalwell acknowledged in 2015 that he had been physically intimate with Fang on several occasions. At the time, Fang helped raise funds for Swalwell’s campaign and helped place an intern in his congressional office.
Why Jensen Huang is strategically important

Jensen Huang’s position would make him a prime target for such a “honey trap” operation. His company has become central to the technological competition between the U.S and China. As AI becomes increasingly important to economic development, military capabilities and national security, moreover, Washington has repeatedly tightened restrictions on advanced AI chip exports to China, hoping to slow its access to computing power.
Beijing is investing heavily in domestic semiconductor development. Yet Chinese companies still need advanced chips to train AI models and build data centers.
From Beijing’s perspective, advanced AI chips matter not only for Chinese technology companies but for future military and technological competition.
This puts Nvidia in a particularly important position and helps explain the national security concerns surrounding Huang.

However, strategic motives do not prove an intelligence operation occurred. Jensen Huang’s importance does not, in itself, establish that he was targeted by a honey trap or that Alice Huang acted for Chinese intelligence. Those are allegations that still require full investigation.
Espionage in the age of AI

Yet it is surely true that in modern politics – just as in ancient China’s rivalries – rivals seek information about opponents, try to influence important decisions and exploit weaknesses to gain strategic advantages.
What has changed is who controls important strategic resources.

In ancient China, influencing a ruler through personal relationships could affect a country’s political and military decisions. Today, approaching a major technology executive could offer access to sensitive technologies.
More than 2,000 years ago, a powerful state could lose its advantage through a ruler’s personal weaknesses. Today, political and technological power are distributed differently.
But as long as important decisions depend on individuals, personal relationships may remain a weakness that rivals can exploit.

articles.title: Extreme weather risk is scaring big corporations away from poorer countries – that hurts the companies, too
articles.author: Jonas Gamso, Associate Professor of International Trade and Global Studies, Arizona State University
paras: When multinational companies decide where to build a factory, open a mine or establish a regional office, they have to consider whether the investment will still be profitable years into the future.

Making that decision increasingly means thinking about risks, like whether surrounding roads will flood, worker safety will be compromised by extreme heat in the summer, and clean water will be available.

As climate change increases the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events around the world, these effects can be especially severe in poorer countries that lack the resources to prepare for disasters or recover quickly after they hit.

I study how political and environmental risks affect international business. In my new book, “Multinational Corporations and Climate Change: Risks, Responsibilities, and Resilience,” I explore how disaster risk is affecting the ways global companies see these climate-vulnerable markets, and how those views are leading some foreign investors to avoid these developing nations altogether.

Low- and middle-income countries aren’t the only ones that suffer when multinational corporations pass them by. The companies themselves also stand to lose out on business opportunities in emerging markets if they pull away.
How climate risk affects foreign investment

Evidence from several studies suggests that multinationals are systematically avoiding investing in the most climate-vulnerable countries. These include my own analysis of 159 countries. Although these studies focus on different samples, they identify the same trend: Countries characterized by greater climate vulnerability received less foreign investment.

The results are not trivial. My book identifies a 12% reduction in foreign direct investment for each 1-point rise in climate vulnerability on a 100-point scale, while holding other relevant factors constant. This vulnerability data measures countries’ exposure to climate hazards as well as their capacity to adapt.
Companies rarely say why they’re avoiding a particular location, but their climate-related concerns occasionally become visible.

For example, Google halted plans to build a US$200 million data center in Chile after an environmental court revoked its construction permit over the likely effects on water supplies and the environment. Similarly, a $1 billion data center proposed in Kenya by Microsoft and the Abu Dhabi-based artificial intelligence company G42 was delayed and ultimately suspended amid concerns about water stress in the area.
Companies have reason to be cautious about climate risks.

One analysis of 71 large publicly traded companies found that firms reporting major flood losses experienced a 5% average decline in shareholder value over the following year, after accounting for broader market movements.
In Vietnam, typhoons and floods caused an estimated $475 million in damage to energy and transportation infrastructure in 2022. Unreliable infrastructure cost companies there about $280 million.

Severe flooding in Thailand in 2011 forced several companies, including Toyota, Nissan and Honda, to temporarily suspend production as factories flooded, shutting down production of parts or vehicles made there.
Costs like those shape where companies choose to invest next.

While climate risk does not stop all investment in climate-vulnerable markets, it does make projects in these nations relatively more expensive, less attractive and more difficult to finance than less risky locations.
Who loses from investor avoidance?

For developing countries, less foreign investment means fewer jobs are created. These countries also have fewer opportunities to benefit from exposure to the new technologies that multinationals bring when they invest abroad.

Those results highlight another way climate change is deepening global inequality. It reduces the economic activity that could support future development, while simultaneously damaging physical infrastructure and threatening human health and well-being.

Developing countries are especially vulnerable to the effects of rising global temperatures, whether for their dependence on agricultural markets, geography or relatively fragile infrastructure. A report from the Climate Impact Lab at the University of Chicago projects that 90% of heat-related deaths in the coming decades will take place in low- and middle-income countries. Similarly, a 2022 study found that around 90% of people exposed to flooding live in developing nations.

Yet poor countries have contributed only a tiny fraction of the emissions that are causing climate change, even as they face the brunt of the damage. For example, African countries are responsible for less than 4% of greenhouse gas emissions globally. But they stand to experience the greatest negative effects of climate change.
Lost opportunities for multinational companies
When a company avoids investing in climate-vulnerable countries, that may reduce its exposure to floods, droughts or extreme heat, but the decision also carries potential costs for the company.

Many of these countries have growing consumer markets, energy resources or critical minerals that multinationals need. Companies that dismiss them as too risky may lose out on promising opportunities.

For example, the Democratic Republic of Congo supplies most of the world’s cobalt, while Indonesia has become the dominant producer of nickel. These countries are highly vulnerable to climate change, which is likely scaring some companies away.

Yet companies with a greater tolerance for risk have established strong positions in those countries’ mineral industries. Thus, more cautious firms may reduce their risk exposure, but they are also surrendering access to important resources and growing markets.
Reducing investor avoidance
There are ways to help companies overcome their climate-risk avoidance so more investment can pour into these countries:

Foreign aid from wealthy countries can help developing countries shore up their roads, ports, electrical grids and water systems before extreme storms or droughts occur. My 2025 study found that climate-vulnerable countries that received more aid for climate adaptation also received more foreign direct investment than those receiving less aid. The result suggests the funding may reassure companies that climate risks are being addressed.

International development banks can share some of the risks by providing climate risk insurance to multinationals. This would offer a safety net to absorb some of the losses if a covered disruption prevents a project from operating as intended. The World Bank already offers similar coverage against political risk incidents, which has given companies confidence to invest in countries such as Kenya, Mozambique and Nigeria.

Better data can give companies more precise information about climate risks. Many risk scores label entire nations as vulnerable or not, even though exposure varies from one city or project site to another. More detailed information about local flood exposure, water availability, heat, infrastructure and adaptation capabilities would allow companies to limit their avoidance to the riskiest areas, instead of bypassing those countries altogether.

Understanding the local risk, insuring companies against risk and helping countries make their infrastructure more resilient to storms, droughts and heat can help boost investment in ways that benefit the companies and spur economic growth and development in climate-vulnerable countries at the same time.
